theme: Let my prayer be counted as incense
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 141. It is an evening prayer of David, asking God to hear, to guard the lips, and to keep the heart from evil. Notice the image of prayer as incense and the unusual request to be corrected.
settingTheScene: Psalm 141 is a psalm of David written in a time of danger, when enemies threatened and temptation pressed. It is a prayer of an individual who feels vulnerable in two ways: to external enemies and to internal temptations. The image of prayer as incense and the lifting of hands as the evening sacrifice would have been strongly associated with the temple. In Revelation, the prayers of the saints are described as incense before the throne (5:8; 8:3-4), and the psalm is the origin of the image.
observation: “O LORD, I call upon you; hasten to me! Give ear to my voice when I call to you!” (v. 1).
“Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice!” (v. 2).
“Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips!” (v. 3).
“Do not let my heart incline to any evil” (v. 4).
“Let a righteous man strike me; let it be a kindness; let him rebuke me; it is oil for my head” (v. 5).
“But my eyes are toward you, O GOD, my Lord; in you I seek refuge; leave me not defenseless!” (v. 8).
“Keep me from the trap that they have laid for me and from the snares of evildoers!” (v. 9).
“Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by safely” (v. 10).
interpretation:
David starts with urgency: “O LORD, I call upon you; hasten to me!” Then he makes a request that shapes the whole psalm: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice!” In the temple, incense was burned on the golden altar morning and evening, and its fragrant smoke rose up to God. David asks that his prayer would be received as acceptably as the evening incense, though he has no temple at the moment. The same image appears in Revelation 5:8, where the elders hold golden bowls of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints,” and in 8:3-4, where an angel offers much incense with the prayers of all the saints.

Then David turns to his lips and heart, an unexpected request when his enemies are pressing in. “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity; and let me not eat of their delicacies!” He knows that the greater danger is not what enemies do to him but what he might do in anger or temptation. He asks God to guard his speech, his desires, and his company.

Verse 5 is surprising: “Let a righteous man strike me; let it be a kindness; let him rebuke me; it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it.” He welcomes correction from a faithful friend. Wounds from a friend are faithful (Proverbs 27:6). Those who want to grow in holiness need people who will tell them the truth. This is the opposite of the wicked, who in verse 4 invite him to feast with them, and whose “delicacies” are the pleasures of sin.

The psalm ends with confident refuge. The leaders of the wicked will be thrown down, and their bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol. “But my eyes are toward you, O GOD, my Lord; in you I seek refuge; leave me not defenseless!” He asks to be kept from the trap and snares. “Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by safely.” In Christ we have the greater sacrifice and intercessor, who ever lives to make intercession for us. Our prayers rise before the throne through his priesthood, and nothing we pray is lost.
connection: Exodus 30:1-9 describes the altar of incense. Luke 1:8-10 shows Zechariah offering incense while the people pray outside. Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4 connect incense and prayer. Proverbs 27:5-6, 9 speaks of rebuke from a friend. Psalm 19:14 and James 3:2-12 pray for guarded speech. Psalm 119:37 asks for eyes turned from vanity. Matthew 6:13 asks to be led not into temptation. Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34 describe Christ’s intercession. Hebrews 13:15 speaks of a sacrifice of praise. Psalm 57:6 and Proverbs 26:27 speak of falling into one’s own trap.
application:
Make this your evening prayer tonight. Lift your hands or bow your head, and offer your prayer as incense.

Ask a trusted friend where they see a blind spot in you. Receive it as “oil for your head.”

Pray for a guard over your lips in a specific conversation you will have tomorrow.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to receive your prayer as incense.
Ask him to guard your mouth and your heart.
Thank him that he hears the cry of the afflicted.
